newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Pakistani, U.N. mediators hold talks with Dostum.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani, U.N. mediators hold talks with Dostum.

text.p: General Abdul Rashid Dostum, head of an alliance opposed to Afghanistan's Islamic Taleban militia, held talks on Wednesday with U.N. and Pakistani mediators seeking to prevent a bloody battle for Kabul.

"We've had very intensive discussions for several hours on the issue of a ceasefire as a first step and the beginning of a political process as a second step," U.N. special envoy Norbert Holl told reporters after the talks at the Qala-i-Jangi Fort, a Dostum base near the northern town of Mazar-i-Sharif.
Holl said there would be a second round of talks. He would then fly on Thursday to the southern city of Kandahar to convey some proposals to the Taleban leadership there.
"Success is far from being guaranteed," he declared.
There was no immediate comment from Dostum or Pakistani Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar, who has been shuttling between Kandahar and Mazar-i-Sharif to try to broker a truce.
Despite the ceasefire talk, witnesses said rival militia pounded each other with artillery, mortar and rocket fire in a battle for heights overlooking one of two roads leading into Kabul.
Forces loyal to ousted government military commander Ahmad Shah Masood have fought their way back towards Kabul after the Taleban drove them from the capital on September 27.
Dostum has sent units of his mainly ethnic Uzbek army to support Masood's fighters, but it is not clear whether Dostum has actually committed his men to the battle.

Masood has called for the demilitarisation of Kabul, ravaged by four years of factional fighting, but Taleban leader Mullah Mohammad Omar told the Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) agency on Tuesday that his movement would defend the capital.

Asked if his discussions had covered the possibility of a U.N. peacekeeping force for Kabul, Holl said: "In the minds of several parties this is pretty high on the agenda, but I am not in a position to pledge anything whatever."
In New York, the U.N. Security Council called on Tuesday for a ceasefire and political negotiations in Afghanistan.
Pakistan has criticised the non-binding U.N. resolution as inadequate and warned against what it called moves to divide its war-shattered neighbour on ethnic lines.
A Foreign Ministry statement on Tuesday said the security council had "shied away" from adopting a binding resolution or imposing an arms embargo, which Islamabad had demanded.

"As such the council's resolution betrays a certain lack of resolve to take urgent and effective measures to end the massive foreign interference, including supply of weapons and equipment to some of the Afghan parties," it said.
It said Pakistan would continue to support peace efforts by the United Nations and the Organisation of Islamic Conference.

The statement did not identify the sources of interference, but Pakistani newspapers have often accused Russia and neighbouring India of aiding the ousted government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani in its fight against the Taleban.
Pakistan denies Rabbani's charges that it supports the Taleban, who now control at least two-thirds of Afghanistan.

The Foreign Ministry, without spelling out the ethnic divide that appears to have developed between the mainly Pashtun Taleban and their Uzbek, Tajik and Hazara foes, voiced "our deep concern on the part of some to accentuate ethnic division for promoting their narrow strategic interests".
"Moves for a permanent division in Afghanistan on ethnic lines need to be universally condemned," it added.
